learningObjective: Explain the difference between saturation and wrap-around handling of out-of-range values in integer quantization.

canonicalClaims.claim: Saturation clamps out-of-range values to the nearest representable extreme (preserving ordinal semantics); wrap-around applies modular arithmetic (destroying signal semantics via unexpected sign flips). Quantization frameworks universally use saturation.
conditions: The context is DNN quantization (not bit-level modular arithmetic).
nonImplications: Does not imply saturation is cost-free — repeated saturation indicates a scale mismatch.
Does not imply wrap-around is never useful — some use cases (checksums, cryptography) require it.

misconceptions.claim: Saturation and wrap-around are equivalent modulo a sign flip.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Saturation preserves monotonicity; wrap-around introduces discontinuities at range boundaries.

misconceptions.claim: Wrap-around is preferred because it preserves the exact bit count of the value.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bit-count preservation is not the goal of quantization; signal preservation is.

misconceptions.claim: Weights use saturation while activations use wrap-around because CUDA integer instructions default to wrap.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both weights and activations use saturation in quantization frameworks; kernel implementations explicitly apply saturation via `min/max` or intrinsics.

misconceptions.claim: Saturation is a training-time behavior that has no runtime performance impact.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Saturation is applied at inference; the branch or `min/max` op is emitted in generated kernels.

implementationFacts: ONNX QuantizeLinear op saturates by definition.
CUDA supplies `__saturatef` and integer saturation intrinsics.
cuBLAS / cuDNN INT8 kernels saturate at write-out.
performanceScenarios: Excessive saturation is a symptom of a too-tight quantization range; recalibrating with a higher percentile threshold helps.
